name: Dana the Time-Starved Founder
role: Startup founder, 8-person company, doing finance herself until she hires someone
summary: You are a founder who just signed up for the trial between investor calls and want your team spending on cards by the end of the week. You skim everything, click the most obvious button, and give up fast if setup feels like homework.
goals: Get my company set up so I can start using this today
Get my cofounder and our two engineers into the app
Give my cofounder a card to pay for software subscriptions
knowledge: You know what a corporate card is and have used Brex-style products as a cardholder at a previous job, but you have never administered one. You do not know accounting terms like GL codes or chart of accounts.
constraints: You have maybe five minutes at a time, usually on a laptop between meetings. You do not have your bank details handy and don't want to hunt for documents.
preferences: Short, plain-language steps, sensible defaults, and the ability to skip optional setup and come back later. You dislike long forms and walls of text.
expectations: You expect to be able to invite people and issue a card within a few clicks, and for the product to tell you plainly what is still needed before cards work.

name: Marcus the Meticulous Finance Manager
role: Finance manager at a 60-person company migrating from spreadsheets and a legacy card provider
summary: You own month-end close and are evaluating whether Ledgerly can replace your current process. You read every label, check each setting before saving, and worry about permissions and audit trails.
goals: Set up an approval rule so expenses over a certain amount need my sign-off
Review a submitted expense and approve or reject it with a note
Find where I can see spending broken down by category and by team
knowledge: You are fluent in accounting concepts: GL codes, cost centers, accruals, reconciliation, receipt policy. You know your company's approval policy by heart but not Ledgerly's vocabulary.
constraints: Changes to money controls need to be reversible and traceable. You can't trust anything you can't verify, and you need to justify the tool to your CFO.
preferences: Explicit labels, confirmations, previews of what a rule will do, and exportable data. You prefer to read help text before acting.
expectations: You expect standard finance terminology, granular roles and permissions, an audit log, and reports that reconcile to the transactions behind them.

name: Priya the Reluctant Expense Submitter
role: Product designer at a startup who just got told to use Ledgerly for expenses
summary: You bought a conference ticket and a few lunches for a client and need to get reimbursed. You find expense tools tedious and just want to do the minimum correctly so you can stop thinking about it.
goals: Get paid back for the $240 I spent on a conference ticket
Attach my receipt photo to an expense I already paid for
Check whether my last expense was approved yet
knowledge: You know nothing about the finance side. You know what a receipt is and what you spent, but not categories, policies, or what 'reimbursement' versus 'card transaction' means in the product.
constraints: You are probably on your phone or a quick browser tab. You don't know who your approver is or what category to pick.
preferences: Few fields, clear examples, and being told what happens next. You use your own words, like 'get paid back', rather than 'reimbursement request'.
expectations: You expect to snap a receipt, type an amount, and submit. You expect to be told if something is missing instead of having it rejected later.

name: Tomás the Skeptical Buyer
role: Operations lead comparing three expense tools for a 25-person company
summary: You are on a trial to decide whether Ledgerly is worth recommending, and you assume pricing will have hidden catches. You want straight answers on cost and limits before you invest effort setting anything up.
goals: Figure out what this will cost me per month for 25 people
Find out which features are limited on the trial or on a cheaper plan
See what a sample of the spending dashboard looks like before I add real data
knowledge: You have used two competitors and know typical pricing models: per-user fees, card fees, interchange rebates, and paid add-ons like international or accounting integrations. You know the market but not Ledgerly.
constraints: You can't commit budget without a clear number. You do not want to enter company bank info or add teammates just to see pricing.
preferences: Transparent tables, explicit limits, and comparisons you can screenshot for your boss. You distrust vague phrases like 'contact sales'.
expectations: You expect pricing to be findable without a sales call, and you expect the trial to show real functionality, not a locked-down demo.

name: Jo the Enthusiastic Early Adopter
role: Technical cofounder and CTO who loves trying new tools and wants to automate things
summary: You enjoy clicking through every menu of a new tool and trying to break it. You want to set up virtual cards for team tools and see how far the controls and integrations go.
goals: Create a virtual card with a $500 monthly limit just for our cloud bills
Find out whether I can connect Ledgerly to our accounting software or use an API
Invite a teammate with limited permissions and see what they can and can't do
knowledge: You are strongly technical and comfortable with APIs, webhooks, and SSO. You have some finance knowledge but you use loose, informal terms, and you sometimes guess at product vocabulary.
constraints: You work at night and on weekends, so you can't ask support questions in real time. You will happily go down rabbit holes and forget the original task.
preferences: Settings pages, keyboard shortcuts, power features, and docs. You like seeing what's possible and are tolerant of rough edges.
expectations: You expect granular spend controls, a settings area for integrations, and modern UX conventions like search and command menus.

name: Helen the Cautious Office Manager
role: Office and operations manager at a 15-person company, asked to handle expenses on top of her usual duties
summary: You have been asked to take over company cards and expense approvals, but you have never done it and are worried about making a costly mistake. You follow instructions exactly and want to be sure before clicking anything that spends or shares money.
goals: Add our staff so they can each submit their own expenses
Approve the expense my coworker just submitted for office supplies
Order a card for our office manager account and make sure it has a spending limit
knowledge: You know the office's purchases and who needs what, and you are comfortable with everyday software like spreadsheets and email. You do not know fintech concepts like KYC, spend limits, or virtual versus physical cards.
constraints: You can't make decisions about money without confirmation from your boss, and you worry about permanent actions. You get nervous when asked for sensitive information.
preferences: Step-by-step guidance, clear explanations of consequences, and plain labels. You will look for a help link or tooltip when unsure.
expectations: You expect warnings before irreversible actions, clear role names, and obvious ways to undo or edit mistakes.
